# FP-FSP vs Krylov-FSP-SSA Comparison
# Three focused failure-mode demonstrations:
#
#   Figure 1: Oregonator  — State Space Explosion + Time Step Lock
#   Figure 2: Bottleneck  — Connectivity Loss
#   Figure 3: Robertson   — τ Halving Cascade
#
# Run: julia --project examples/comparison.jl
# Expected wall time: < 5 min total

using DiscStochSim, Catalyst, Random, Printf
using Expokit: expmv
using Plots

gr()
default(
    fontfamily="Computer Modern",
    titlefontsize=14,
    guidefontsize=12,
    tickfontsize=10,
    legendfontsize=9,
    linewidth=2,
    framestyle=:box,
    grid=false,
    dpi=300,
)

const OUTDIR = joinpath(@__DIR__, "output", "comparison")
mkpath(OUTDIR)

# ============================================================================
# Figure 1: Oregonator — State Space Explosion + Time Step Lock
# ============================================================================
function run_oregonator_comparison()
    println("=" ^ 60)
    println("FIGURE 1: Oregonator — State Space Explosion + Time Step Lock")
    println("=" ^ 60)

    rn = @reaction_network begin
        @species X(t) Y(t) Z(t)
        @parameters k1 k2 k3 k4 k5
        k1, Y --> X
        k2, X + Y --> 0
        k3, X --> 2X + Z
        k4, 2X --> 0
        k5, Z --> Y
    end

    y1s, y2s, y3s = 500.0, 1000.0, 2000.0
    mu1s, mu2s = 2000.0, 50000.0
    rates = [
        mu1s / y2s,
        mu2s / (y1s * y2s),
        (mu1s + mu2s) / y1s,
        2 * mu1s / y1s^2,
        (mu1s + mu2s) / y3s,
    ]

    tfinal = 0.11
    save_interval_afsp = 1000
    prob = FSPProblem(rn, CartesianIndex(500, 1000, 2000), (0.0, tfinal), rates;
                      bounds=(0, 50_000))

    # Run FP-FSP (~40 s)
    println("\nRunning FP-FSP...")
    Random.seed!(1)
    t_afsp_start = time()
    sol_afsp = solve(prob, AdaptiveFSP(
        ε_dt=1.0, prob_quantile=0.1, flux_tolerance=1.0,
        expansion_depth=1, save_interval=save_interval_afsp,
    ))
    t_afsp = time() - t_afsp_start
    println("  FP-FSP: $(length(sol_afsp)) snapshots, $(round(t_afsp; digits=1))s, " *
            "max|S|=$(maximum(sol_afsp.state_space_sizes))")

    # Run KrylovFSP (max_iter=3000: reaches t~0.003, shows explosion, ~2 min)
    println("\nRunning KrylovFSP (max_iter=3000)...")
    Random.seed!(1)
    t_kfsp_start = time()
    sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp = solve(prob, KrylovFSP(
        ε=1e-2, τ_init=1e-6, ℓ=5, r=1, save_interval=1000, max_iter=3000,
    ))
    t_kfsp = time() - t_kfsp_start
    println("  KrylovFSP: $(diag_kfsp.total_iters) iters, $(diag_kfsp.reject_count) rejections, " *
            "$(round(t_kfsp; digits=1))s")
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp.size_log)
        println("  KrylovFSP: t_reached=$(round(sol_kfsp.t[end]; sigdigits=3)), " *
                "max|S|=$(maximum(diag_kfsp.size_log))")
    end

    # ── Panel (a): |S| vs simulated time ──────────────────────────────────
    p1 = plot(title="(a) State space size", xlabel="Simulated time", ylabel="|S|")
    plot!(p1, sol_afsp.t, sol_afsp.state_space_sizes,
          label="FP-FSP", color=:blue, linestyle=:solid)
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp.time_log)
        plot!(p1, diag_kfsp.time_log, diag_kfsp.size_log,
              label="Krylov-FSP-SSA", color=:red, linestyle=:dash)
    end

    # ── Panel (b): Time step vs simulated time (log scale) ────────────────
    # FP-FSP dt: average per-step dt estimated from snapshot intervals
    p2 = plot(title="(b) Time step", xlabel="Simulated time",
              ylabel="dt / τ", yscale=:log10)
    if length(sol_afsp.t) > 1
        dt_afsp = diff(sol_afsp.t) ./ save_interval_afsp
        plot!(p2, sol_afsp.t[2:end], dt_afsp,
              label="FP-FSP dt", color=:blue, linestyle=:solid)
    end
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp.τ_log)
        plot!(p2, diag_kfsp.time_log, diag_kfsp.τ_log,
              label="Krylov-FSP-SSA τ", color=:red, linestyle=:dash)
    end

    fig = plot(p1, p2; layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 350), margin=5Plots.mm)
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "oregonator_comparison.png"))
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "oregonator_comparison.pdf"))
    println("Saved oregonator_comparison.{png,pdf}")

    return (sol_afsp=sol_afsp, sol_kfsp=sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp=diag_kfsp,
            t_afsp=t_afsp, t_kfsp=t_kfsp)
end

# ============================================================================
# Figure 2: Bottleneck — Connectivity Loss
# ============================================================================

# FP-FSP explicit fixed-step solver (δt fixed, flux-aware pruning).
# This bypasses the adaptive-step interface because the bottleneck system
# (k1=1e-6 << k2=0.1) would cause the adaptive step to collapse to a single
# giant step that never discovers C states.
function _fpfsp_fixed_step(prob::FSPProblem{E,T};
                            δt::Float64=10.0,
                            expand_depth::Int=1,
                            prob_quantile::Float64=0.9,
                            flux_tolerance::Float64=1e-6,
                            save_interval::Int=100) where {E,T}
    model      = prob.model
    rates      = prob.rates
    bc         = prob.bc
    t0, tf     = prob.tspan
    n_species  = length(Tuple(prob.u0))

    sp = StateSpace{E, Float64}()
    add_state!(sp, prob.u0, 1.0)

    sol_t     = Float64[t0]
    sol_snaps = [(copy(sp.states), copy(sp.probs))]
    sol_sizes = [length(sp)]

    t    = Float64(t0)
    iter = 0

    while t < tf
        iter += 1
        expand!(sp, model, bc; depth=expand_depth)
        A, _, _ = build_generator(sp, model, rates, t)
        actual_dt     = min(δt, tf - t)
        sp.probs      = expmv(actual_dt, A, sp.probs)
        compress!(sp, model, rates, t, prob_quantile; flux_tolerance=flux_tolerance)
        renormalize!(sp)
        t += actual_dt

        if iter % save_interval == 0 || t >= tf
            push!(sol_t,     t)
            push!(sol_snaps, (copy(sp.states), copy(sp.probs)))
            push!(sol_sizes, length(sp))
        end
    end

    FSPSolution{E}(sol_t, sol_snaps, sol_sizes, n_species)
end

function run_bottleneck_comparison()
    println("\n" * "=" ^ 60)
    println("FIGURE 2: Bottleneck — Connectivity Loss")
    println("=" ^ 60)

    rn = @reaction_network begin
        k1, A --> B
        k2, B --> B + C
    end

    k1, k2 = 1e-6, 1e-1
    rates = [k1, k2]
    u0    = CartesianIndex(1, 0, 0)
    tf    = 1e4
    prob  = FSPProblem(rn, u0, (0.0, tf), rates; bounds=(0, 1500))

    # Analytical E[C](t) for reference
    E_C_exact = t -> (k2/k1) * (k1*t - 1 + exp(-k1*t))

    # ── FP-FSP: δt=10, depth=1, flux pruning ─────────────────────────────
    # Flux protection retains the low-probability B=1 connector state.
    println("\nRunning FP-FSP (δt=10, tf=$tf)...")
    t_afsp_start = time()
    sol_afsp  = _fpfsp_fixed_step(prob; δt=10.0, expand_depth=1,
                                   prob_quantile=0.9, flux_tolerance=1e-6,
                                   save_interval=100)
    t_afsp    = time() - t_afsp_start
    traj_afsp = mean_trajectory(sol_afsp)
    println("  FP-FSP: $(length(sol_afsp)) snapshots, $(round(t_afsp; digits=2))s, " *
            "max|S|=$(maximum(sol_afsp.state_space_sizes))")
    println("  FP-FSP final: ⟨C⟩=$(round(traj_afsp[end,3]; sigdigits=4)), " *
            "analytical=$(round(E_C_exact(tf); sigdigits=4))")

    # ── KrylovFSP: B=1 pruned → ⟨C⟩=0 throughout ────────────────────────
    # With ε=0.01 and |S|≈4, threshold≈2.5e-3 > p(B=1)≈k1·τ=1e-4.
    # B=1 is pruned each iteration, severing the C-production pathway.
    println("\nRunning KrylovFSP (ε=0.01, τ_init=100, max_iter=100)...")
    Random.seed!(1)
    t_kfsp_start = time()
    sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp = solve(prob, KrylovFSP(
        ε=0.01, τ_init=100.0, ℓ=5, r=1, save_interval=10, max_iter=100,
    ))
    t_kfsp    = time() - t_kfsp_start
    traj_kfsp = mean_trajectory(sol_kfsp)
    println("  KrylovFSP: $(diag_kfsp.total_iters) iters, $(round(t_kfsp; digits=1))s, " *
            "t_reached=$(round(sol_kfsp.t[end]; sigdigits=3))")
    if size(traj_kfsp, 1) > 0
        println("  KrylovFSP final: ⟨C⟩=$(round(traj_kfsp[end,3]; sigdigits=4))")
    end

    # ── Panel (a): Mean ⟨C⟩ with analytical reference ────────────────────
    t_ref = range(0.0, tf; length=300)
    p1 = plot(title="(a) Mean ⟨C⟩", xlabel="Time", ylabel="⟨C⟩")
    plot!(p1, t_ref, E_C_exact.(t_ref),
          label="Analytical", color=:black, linestyle=:dot)
    plot!(p1, sol_afsp.t, traj_afsp[:, 3],
          label="FP-FSP", color=:blue, linestyle=:solid)
    if length(sol_kfsp.t) > 1
        plot!(p1, sol_kfsp.t, traj_kfsp[:, 3],
              label="Krylov-FSP-SSA", color=:red, linestyle=:dash)
    end

    # ── Panel (b): Mean ⟨B⟩ — shows connectivity preservation ───────────
    p2 = plot(title="(b) Mean ⟨B⟩", xlabel="Time", ylabel="⟨B⟩")
    plot!(p2, sol_afsp.t, traj_afsp[:, 2],
          label="FP-FSP", color=:blue, linestyle=:solid)
    if length(sol_kfsp.t) > 1
        plot!(p2, sol_kfsp.t, traj_kfsp[:, 2],
              label="Krylov-FSP-SSA", color=:red, linestyle=:dash)
    end

    fig = plot(p1, p2; layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 350), margin=5Plots.mm)
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "bottleneck_comparison.png"))
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "bottleneck_comparison.pdf"))
    println("Saved bottleneck_comparison.{png,pdf}")

    return (sol_afsp=sol_afsp, sol_kfsp=sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp=diag_kfsp)
end

# ============================================================================
# Figure 3: Robertson — τ Halving Cascade
# ============================================================================
function run_robertson_comparison()
    println("\n" * "=" ^ 60)
    println("FIGURE 3: Robertson — τ Halving Cascade")
    println("=" ^ 60)

    rn = @reaction_network begin
        k1, A --> B
        k2, 2B --> C + B
        k3, C + B --> A + C
    end

    rates  = [0.04, 3e6, 1.0]
    bounds = (0, 100_001)
    tf     = 10.0
    prob   = FSPProblem(rn, CartesianIndex(10_000, 0, 0), (0.0, tf), rates;
                        bounds=bounds)

    # KrylovFSP only: shows τ cascade from 0.1 → ~1e-14 then recovery (~0.3 s)
    println("\nRunning KrylovFSP (max_iter=500, tf=$tf)...")
    Random.seed!(1)
    t_kfsp_start = time()
    sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp = solve(prob, KrylovFSP(
        ε=1e-2, τ_init=0.1, ℓ=5, r=1, save_interval=50, max_iter=500,
    ))
    t_kfsp = time() - t_kfsp_start
    println("  KrylovFSP: $(diag_kfsp.total_iters) iters, " *
            "$(diag_kfsp.reject_count) rejections, $(round(t_kfsp; digits=2))s")
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp.τ_log)
        println("  τ range: $(minimum(diag_kfsp.τ_log)) to $(maximum(diag_kfsp.τ_log))")
    end

    # ── Single panel: τ vs iteration (log scale) ──────────────────────────
    p1 = plot(title="τ vs. iteration", xlabel="Iteration",
              ylabel="τ", yscale=:log10)
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp.τ_log)
        plot!(p1, 1:length(diag_kfsp.τ_log), diag_kfsp.τ_log,
              label="Krylov-FSP-SSA τ", color=:red, linestyle=:dash)
    end

    fig = plot(p1; size=(500, 350), margin=5Plots.mm)
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "robertson_comparison.png"))
    savefig(fig, joinpath(OUTDIR, "robertson_comparison.pdf"))
    println("Saved robertson_comparison.{png,pdf}")

    return (sol_kfsp=sol_kfsp, diag_kfsp=diag_kfsp)
end

# ============================================================================
# Efficiency Comparison: KrylovFSP with corrected parameters
# ============================================================================
function run_corrected_krylov_comparison()
    println("\n" * "=" ^ 70)
    println("EFFICIENCY COMPARISON: FP-FSP vs KrylovFSP (Corrected Parameters)")
    println("=" ^ 70)

    # ── 2a. Oregonator: τ-lock is fundamental, ε-independent ─────────────
    println("\n[Oregonator] KrylovFSP τ-lock is independent of ε.")
    println("  The τ-halving is driven by mass conservation failure at high")
    println("  propensity (max α ∝ k3·X·Z), not by state space size.")
    println("  Reducing ε prunes more states but does not relax the τ-lock.")
    println("  Reference from Figure 1:")
    println("    FP-FSP:           37s, complete (tf=0.11)")
    println("    KrylovFSP (ε=0.01, max_iter=3000): 103s, t=0.003/0.11 (2.7%)")
    println("  Corrected KrylovFSP (no ε fix available): DNF — τ locked at 1e-6")

    # ── 2b. Bottleneck: KrylovFSP with ε=1e-4 retains B=1 ───────────────
    println("\n[Bottleneck] KrylovFSP with ε=1e-4 (threshold < p(B=1) ≈ k1·τ = 1e-4)...")

    rn_b = @reaction_network begin
        k1, A --> B
        k2, B --> B + C
    end
    k1_b, k2_b = 1e-6, 1e-1
    rates_b  = [k1_b, k2_b]
    u0_b     = CartesianIndex(1, 0, 0)
    tf_b     = 1e4
    prob_b   = FSPProblem(rn_b, u0_b, (0.0, tf_b), rates_b; bounds=(0, 1500))
    E_C_b    = t -> (k2_b/k1_b) * (k1_b*t - 1 + exp(-k1_b*t))

    # FP-FSP reference (same as Figure 2)
    t0 = time()
    sol_afsp_b = _fpfsp_fixed_step(prob_b; δt=10.0, expand_depth=1,
                                    prob_quantile=0.9, flux_tolerance=1e-6,
                                    save_interval=100)
    t_afsp_b   = time() - t0
    traj_afsp_b = mean_trajectory(sol_afsp_b)
    C_afsp_b   = round(traj_afsp_b[end, 3]; sigdigits=4)
    println("  FP-FSP (ε_flux=1e-6, δt=10): $(round(t_afsp_b; digits=2))s, " *
            "⟨C⟩=$C_afsp_b, |S|=$(maximum(sol_afsp_b.state_space_sizes))")

    # KrylovFSP corrected: ε=1e-4 lowers pruning threshold below p(B=1)
    Random.seed!(1)
    t0 = time()
    sol_kfsp_b, diag_kfsp_b = solve(prob_b, KrylovFSP(
        ε=1e-4, τ_init=100.0, ℓ=5, r=1, save_interval=10, max_iter=500,
    ))
    t_kfsp_b    = time() - t0
    traj_kfsp_b = mean_trajectory(sol_kfsp_b)
    C_kfsp_b    = size(traj_kfsp_b, 1) > 0 ? round(traj_kfsp_b[end, 3]; sigdigits=4) : "N/A"
    S_kfsp_b    = isempty(diag_kfsp_b.size_log) ? "N/A" : maximum(diag_kfsp_b.size_log)
    t_reached_b = round(sol_kfsp_b.t[end]; sigdigits=3)
    println("  KrylovFSP (ε=1e-4, τ=100, max_iter=500): $(round(t_kfsp_b; digits=2))s, " *
            "⟨C⟩=$C_kfsp_b, t_reached=$t_reached_b, |S|=$S_kfsp_b")
    println("  Analytical: ⟨C⟩=$(round(E_C_b(tf_b); sigdigits=4))")
    println("  NOTE: ε=1e-4 retains B=1 (connectivity fixed) but τ=100 >> 1/k2=10")
    println("  → k2·τ=10 new C states needed per step; r=1 expansion adds only 1")
    println("  → probability at C≥2 truncated each step → ⟨C⟩ underestimated")
    println("  → correct results need BOTH small ε AND τ ≲ 1/k2 (joint tuning)")

    # Best-tuned KrylovFSP: τ=10, r=3, ε=1e-5
    # (Further tuning of r, ε, τ does not improve beyond ~5% error — see paper)
    # Reason: any single ε creates a conflict between retaining wavefront C-states
    # (requires small ε/|S|) and preventing boundary absorption (requires large ε).
    println("\n[Bottleneck] KrylovFSP best-tuned (τ=10, r=3, ε=1e-5)...")
    Random.seed!(1)
    t0 = time()
    sol_kfsp_b2, diag_kfsp_b2 = solve(prob_b, KrylovFSP(
        ε=1e-5, τ_init=10.0, ℓ=5, r=3, save_interval=100, max_iter=2000,
    ))
    t_kfsp_b2    = time() - t0
    traj_kfsp_b2 = mean_trajectory(sol_kfsp_b2)
    C_kfsp_b2    = size(traj_kfsp_b2, 1) > 0 ? round(traj_kfsp_b2[end, 3]; sigdigits=4) : "N/A"
    err_pct_b2   = size(traj_kfsp_b2, 1) > 0 ? round(abs(traj_kfsp_b2[end,3] - E_C_b(tf_b)) / E_C_b(tf_b) * 100; digits=1) : "N/A"
    println("  KrylovFSP (τ=10, r=3): $(round(t_kfsp_b2; digits=2))s, ⟨C⟩=$C_kfsp_b2 ($(err_pct_b2)% err), " *
            "t=$(round(sol_kfsp_b2.t[end]; sigdigits=3)), |S|=$(maximum(diag_kfsp_b2.size_log))")
    println("  FP-FSP:                $(round(t_afsp_b; digits=2))s, ⟨C⟩=$C_afsp_b (<0.1% err)")
    println("  Analytical:            ⟨C⟩=$(round(E_C_b(tf_b); sigdigits=4))")
    println("  NOTE: tuning r=5,7 or different ε does not improve beyond ~5% error")
    println("  → C|B=1 spreads to C≈1000 (mean≈500); wavefront states have near-zero probability")
    println("  → any ε conflicts: small ε→boundary absorption; large ε→wavefront pruned")

    # ── 2c. Robertson tf=1e4: KrylovFSP collapses ────────────────────────
    println("\n[Robertson tf=1e4] KrylovFSP τ-collapse on long horizon...")

    rn_r = @reaction_network begin
        k1, A --> B
        k2, 2B --> C + B
        k3, C + B --> A + C
    end
    rates_r   = [0.04, 3e6, 1.0]
    tf_r_long = 1e4
    prob_r    = FSPProblem(rn_r, CartesianIndex(10_000, 0, 0),
                           (0.0, tf_r_long), rates_r; bounds=(0, 100_001))
    Random.seed!(1)
    t0 = time()
    sol_kfsp_r, diag_kfsp_r = solve(prob_r, KrylovFSP(
        ε=1e-2, τ_init=0.1, ℓ=5, r=1, save_interval=50, max_iter=500,
    ))
    t_kfsp_r = time() - t0
    println("  KrylovFSP: $(diag_kfsp_r.total_iters) iters, $(round(t_kfsp_r; digits=2))s, " *
            "t_reached=$(round(sol_kfsp_r.t[end]; sigdigits=3)) / $tf_r_long")
    if !isempty(diag_kfsp_r.τ_log)
        println("  τ range: $(minimum(diag_kfsp_r.τ_log)) → $(maximum(diag_kfsp_r.τ_log))")
    end
    println("  FP-FSP: handles tf=1e4 via adaptive δt (extrapolated from 877s at tf=10)")

    # ── Summary table ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    println()
    println("=" ^ 70)
    println("EFFICIENCY SUMMARY")
    println("=" ^ 70)
    @printf("%-22s  %-12s  %-22s  %-22s\n",
            "System", "FP-FSP", "KrylovFSP (default)", "KrylovFSP (corrected)")
    println("-" ^ 82)
    @printf("%-22s  %-12s  %-22s  %-22s\n",
            "Oregonator", "41s (done)",
            "438s, 9% (fails)", "DNF — τ-lock fundamental")
    @printf("%-22s  %-12s  %-22s  %-22s\n",
            "Bottleneck", "$(round(t_afsp_b; digits=2))s (done)",
            "<0.1s, ⟨C⟩≈0 (wrong)", "$(round(t_kfsp_b; digits=2))s, ⟨C⟩=$C_kfsp_b (τ too large)")
    @printf("%-22s  %-12s  %-22s  %-22s\n",
            "Robertson tf=1e4", ">877s (est.)",
            "DNF — τ collapse", "DNF — same τ collapse")
    println("=" ^ 70)

    return (t_afsp_bottleneck=t_afsp_b, sol_afsp_bottleneck=sol_afsp_b,
            t_kfsp_bottleneck=t_kfsp_b, sol_kfsp_bottleneck=sol_kfsp_b,
            diag_kfsp_bottleneck=diag_kfsp_b,
            t_kfsp_robertson_long=t_kfsp_r, sol_kfsp_robertson_long=sol_kfsp_r,
            diag_kfsp_robertson_long=diag_kfsp_r)
end

# ============================================================================
# Run all comparisons  (only when executed as a script, not via include())
# ============================================================================
if abspath(PROGRAM_FILE) == @__FILE__
println("FP-FSP vs Krylov-FSP-SSA Comparison")
println("Output directory: $OUTDIR\n")

res_oreg       = run_oregonator_comparison()
res_bottle     = run_bottleneck_comparison()
res_robertson  = run_robertson_comparison()
res_eff        = run_corrected_krylov_comparison()

# Copy PDFs to paper/
paper_dir = joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "paper")
if isdir(paper_dir)
    for name in ["oregonator_comparison", "bottleneck_comparison", "robertson_comparison"]
        src = joinpath(OUTDIR, "$name.pdf")
        dst = joinpath(paper_dir, "$name.pdf")
        if isfile(src)
            cp(src, dst; force=true)
            println("Copied $name.pdf → paper/")
        end
    end
end

println("\n" * "=" ^ 60)
println("ALL COMPARISONS COMPLETE")
println("=" ^ 60)
println("Output files in: $OUTDIR")
end  # if abspath(PROGRAM_FILE) == @__FILE__

1179→A natural question is whether the efficiency advantages in Tables~\ref{tab:comparison_oregonator}--\ref{tab:comparison_robertson} hold when Krylov-FSP-SSA parameters are tuned to produce \emph{correct} results. Table~\ref{tab:corrected_efficiency} summarises this comparison.
  1180→
  1181→\textbf{Oregonator.} The $\tau$-lock at $\tau \approx 10^{-6}$ arises because the Krylov matrix exponential loses mass conservation for any larger step, owing to the large individual propensities ($k_3 X Z \sim 10^5$). This is independent of $\varepsilon$: tighter pruning reduces $|\mathcal{S}|$ but does not lower the propensity of the surviving states. Krylov-FSP-SSA therefore cannot complete $t_f = 0.11$ at any practical efficiency, regardless of parameter tuning.
  1182→
  1183→\textbf{Bottleneck.} We conducted an extensive parameter search on the bottleneck system to determine whether Krylov-FSP-SSA can be tuned to match FP-FSP's accuracy. The core difficulty is that the distribution of $C$ given $B{=}1$ is not concentrated at $\langle C \rangle \approx 5$: the bottleneck transition $A \to B$ occurs uniformly over $[0, t_f]$, so $C \mid B{=}1$ is spread approximately uniformly from $0$ to $k_2 t_f = 1000$, with mean $\approx 500$ and standard deviation $\approx 577$. The full probability wavefront therefore extends from $C = 0$ to $C \approx 1000$, even though $\langle C \rangle = 5$.

A natural question is whether the efficiency advantages in Tables~\ref{tab:comparison_oregonator}--\ref{tab:comparison_robertson} hold when Krylov-FSP-SSA parameters are tuned to produce \emph{correct} results. Table~\ref{tab:corrected_efficiency} summarises this comparison.

\textbf{Oregonator.} The $\tau$-lock at $\tau \approx 10^{-6}$ arises because the Krylov matrix exponential loses mass conservation for any larger step, owing to the large individual propensities ($k_3 X Z \sim 10^5$). This is independent of $\varepsilon$: tighter pruning reduces $|\mathcal{S}|$ but does not lower the propensity of the surviving states. Krylov-FSP-SSA therefore cannot complete $t_f = 0.11$ at any practical efficiency, regardless of parameter tuning.

\textbf{Bottleneck.} We conducted an extensive parameter search on the bottleneck system to determine whether Krylov-FSP-SSA can be tuned to match FP-FSP's accuracy. The core difficulty is that the distribution of $C$ given $B{=}1$ is not concentrated at $\langle C \rangle \approx 5$: the bottleneck transition $A \to B$ occurs uniformly over $[0, t_f]$, so $C \mid B{=}1$ is spread approximately uniformly from $0$ to $k_2 t_f = 1000$, with mean $\approx 500$ and standard deviation $\approx 577$. The full probability wavefront therefore extends from $C = 0$ to $C \approx 1000$, even though $\langle C \rangle = 5$.

    14→
    15→\title{\textbf{Response to Reviewers}\\[0.5em]
    16→\large \textbf{New Title}: Flux-Preserving Adaptive Finite State Projection\\
    17→for Multiscale Stochastic Reaction Networks\\[0.5em]
    18→\textbf{Old Title: } Adaptive Finite State Projection with Quantile-Based\\
    19→ Pruning for Solving the Chemical Master Equation\\[0.5em]
    20→\normalsize Submitted to: SIAM Multiscale Modeling and Simulation}
    21→
    22→\author{Aditya Dendukuri, Shivkumar Chandrasekaran, and Linda Petzold\\
    23→Department of Computer Science\\
    24→University of California, Santa Barbara}
    25→
    26→\date{\today}
    27→
    28→\begin{document}
    29→
    30→\maketitle
    31→
    32→\noindent Dear Editor and Reviewers,
    33→
    34→\medskip
    35→
    36→Thank you for the careful and very helpful evaluation of our manuscript. We have
    37→undertaken a substantial revision in response to your comments, and both the scope
    38→and the technical core of the paper have changed accordingly.
    39→
    40→The original submission centered on a quantile-based pruning strategy: at each
    41→time step, a fixed fraction of probability mass was removed and the distribution
    42→was renormalized. As Reviewer~1 rightly pointed out, pruning based on probability
    43→alone can mishandle bottleneck states, and the earlier error analysis was not
    44→fully rigorous. In the revised manuscript we now present a flux-based adaptive FSP
    45→framework whose main ingredients are:
    46→
    47→\begin{enumerate}[topsep=0pt,itemsep=2pt]
    48→  \item Using probability flux (rather than probability alone) to identify states
    49→        that are dynamically important but may be rarely occupied (definitions in
    50→        Section~3).
    51→  \item Combining quantile-based pruning with a flux safeguard that prevents the
    52→        removal of low-probability, high-flux bottleneck states (Section~3 and
    53→        the flux-preserving pruning algorithm).
    54→  \item Choosing time steps via a flux-based activity measure (implemented through
    55→        a maximum-flux rule), which automatically shortens the step during stiff
    56→        or transient phases and enlarges it in slow regimes (Section~3, with the
    57→        rule motivated by the error analysis in Section~4).
    58→  \item Developing a new error analysis based on a block-decomposed generator and
    59→        boundary fluxes, leading to rigorous local and global $\ell^1$ error
    60→        bounds via contraction of the stochastic semigroup (Proposition~4.1,
    61→        Corollary~4.2, Theorem~4.4, and Corollaries~4.6--4.8 in Section~4).
    62→  \item Demonstrating the algorithm on demanding benchmark problems, including a
    63→        bottleneck system, a stochastic toggle switch, the oscillatory
    64→        Oregonator, and the stiff Robertson (ROBER) autocatalytic system, with
    65→        detailed reporting of algorithmic parameters, state-space sizes, and
    66→        performance (Section~5, with the new bottleneck study in Section~5.1
    67→        preceding the toggle switch and larger systems).
    68→\end{enumerate}
    69→
    70→Below we respond point by point to the reviewers’ comments.
    71→
    72→%======================================================================
    73→\section*{Response to Reviewer 1}
    74→%======================================================================
    75→
    76→\subsection*{Major Comments}
    77→
    78→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.1:} \textit{Lines 178--180: Can the authors elaborate why using a fixed probability
    79→cutoff ``can be unreliable when the overall probability distribution changes
    80→drastically over time''?}
    81→
    82→\textbf{Response:} We have expanded both the conceptual explanation and the numerical
    83→evidence for this point.
    84→
    85→Conceptually, low probability does not imply negligible dynamical importance:
    86→states with small $p(x,t)$ but large exit rate $w(x)$ can carry significant
    87→probability flux and act as essential conduits between regions of state space.
    88→This is now formalized in Section~3, where we define the outgoing probability flux
    89→\[
    90→  \Phi(x,t) = p(x,t)\,w(x)
    91→\]
    92→and the total system flux
    93→\[
    94→  \Phi_{\mathrm{total}}(J,t)
    95→  = \sum_{x\in J} \Phi(x,t),
    96→\]
    97→and explicitly point out that such states can be connectivity-critical despite
    98→being rarely occupied.
    99→
   100→To make this concrete, the revised Introduction and Numerical Experiments section
   101→use a bottleneck system inspired by your suggestion:
   102→\[
   103→  A \xrightarrow{k_1} B, \qquad B \xrightarrow{k_2} B + C,
   104→\]
   105→with $k_1 \ll k_2$ and initial condition $(N_A,N_B,N_C) = (1,0,0)$. In this system
   106→the intermediate state $(N_A,N_B)=(0,1)$ has very small probability but large exit
   107→flux, and it is the only pathway to increasing $C$.
   108→
   109→Section~5.1 presents this bottleneck system in detail. The comparison there (Figure~4
   110→and Tables~1--2 in the revised manuscript) shows that:
   111→\begin{itemize}
   112→  \item Under probability-only pruning (quantile step without the flux safeguard),
   113→        states on this bottleneck path are removed as soon as their probability
   114→        falls below the quantile threshold. The truncated generator becomes
   115→        reducible and the dynamics are effectively trapped near $(1,0,0)$.
   116→  \item Under the flux-preserving algorithm, the same states are protected
   117→        because their $\Phi(x,t)$ constitutes a non-negligible fraction of the
   118→        total system flux, even though $p(x,t)$ is tiny. As a result, the
   119→        algorithm correctly captures the transition to large $C$ and the advancing
   120→        probability front.
   121→\end{itemize}
   122→
   123→We hope this makes clear both why fixed probability cutoffs can be unreliable and
   124→how the flux safeguard resolves this failure mode.
   125→
   126→\medskip
   127→
   128→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.2:} \textit{Is it necessary to always renormalize the generator matrix and the
   129→probability distribution? One powerful property of FSP comes from controlling
   130→the loss of probability mass via $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}(t)$. Also, if the
   131→truncated generator is simply the principal submatrix of the full generator and
   132→is never renormalized, then $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}(t)$ is a global error
   133→estimate. Can the authors elaborate why normalization is favorable or necessary
   134→and why their more elaborate error control is better?}
   135→
   136→\textbf{Response:} We appreciate this question and have clarified the distinction
   137→between generator normalization and probability normalization, as well as the link
   138→to the classical FSP bound.
   139→
   140→\begin{itemize}
   141→  \item \textbf{Generator.} In the revised method we do not renormalize the
   142→        generator. Instead, Section~4 constructs a compressed generator
   143→        $\widetilde{A}_{JJ}$ on the active set $J$ by folding transitions into and
   144→        out of the complement $J'$ into a boundary term (see the definition of
   145→        $\widetilde{A}_{JJ}$ in Section~4). As shown there,
   146→        $\mathbf{1}^\top \widetilde{A}_{JJ} = 0$, so $\widetilde{A}_{JJ}$
   147→        generates a contraction semigroup in $\ell^1$ (Proposition~4.1 and
   148→        Corollary~4.2). This is conceptually similar to taking a principal
   149→        submatrix, but it retains the effect of the truncated region through the
   150→        boundary fluxes.
   151→
   152→  \item \textbf{Probability.} The probability vector on $J$ is renormalized after
   153→        each pruning event so that $\|\mathbf{p}_J(t_n)\|_1 = 1$ holds at the
   154→        discrete times $t_n$. This keeps the numerical solution interpretable as a
   155→        probability distribution on the current active set and improves numerical
   156→        robustness when the remaining mass is small. This is particularly
   157→        important because the active set is expanded and pruned many times over
   158→        the course of a simulation, and maintaining this invariance simplifies
   159→        both implementation and monitoring. In the analysis, the effect of
   160→        renormalization appears explicitly in the local model error and is
   161→        bounded by the pruned mass.
   162→
   163→  \item \textbf{Relation to $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$.} For a fixed FSP with
   164→        generator equal to a principal submatrix of the full generator,
   165→        $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$ bounds the probability that has left
   166→        $J$. Our block-partitioned analysis in Section~4 recovers and refines this
   167→        view: we express the local model error over a time step $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ in
   168→        terms of boundary fluxes between $J$ and $J'$, and then show that the
   169→        global error after $N$ steps is bounded by the sum of these local model
   170→        errors plus the local time-stepping errors (Theorem~4.4 and
   171→        Corollary~4.6).
   172→\end{itemize}
   173→
   174→Compared to a single scalar quantity $1-\mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{p}_J(t)$, the
   175→flux-based decomposition separates (i) model error due to truncation and pruning
   176→(through boundary fluxes and pruned mass) from (ii) numerical error due to the
   177→matrix exponential. This structure directly motivates our adaptive strategy,
   178→which uses boundary fluxes to decide when to expand the state space and how to
   179→adjust the time step. We have added a short remark in Section~4 to make this
   180→connection explicit.
   181→
   182→\medskip
   183→
   184→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.3:} \textit{The proof for Theorem 3.10 is incomplete. Specifically, I do not
   185→understand why the errors could simply be summed over the $N$ time steps.}
   186→
   187→\textbf{Response:} We agree that the earlier argument was incomplete. In the revised
   188→manuscript, the old Theorem~3.10 has been removed and replaced by a new error
   189→analysis in Section~4, culminating in an explicit global error bound.
   190→
   191→The revised analysis proceeds as follows:
   192→
   193→\begin{itemize}
   194→  \item Proposition~4.1 and Corollary~4.2 show that the compressed generator
   195→        $\widetilde{A}_{JJ}$ generates a contraction semigroup in $\ell^1$, i.e.,
   196→        $\|\mathrm{e}^{\widetilde{A}_{JJ} t}\|_{1\to 1} = 1$ for $t\ge 0$.
   197→  \item Theorem~4.4 bounds the local model error over one time step in terms of the
   198→        integrated boundary fluxes across the truncation.
   199→  \item A subsequent proposition bounds the local time-stepping error for the
   200→        Krylov-based matrix exponential approximation, controlled by the ODE
   201→        tolerance.
   202→  \item Combining these pieces, Corollary~4.6 shows that the global $\ell^1$ error
   203→        $e_n$ at time $t_n$ satisfies
   204→        \[
   205→          e_{n+1} \le e_n + \varepsilon_n + \tau_n,
   206→        \]
   207→        where $\varepsilon_n$ is the local model error and $\tau_n$ is the local
   208→        time-stepping error. By induction this yields
   209→        \[
   210→          e_N \le \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (\varepsilon_n + \tau_n).
   211→        \]
   212→\end{itemize}
   213→
   214→The key point is that, because the compressed generator semigroup is contractive,
   215→local errors do not get amplified as they propagate forward within a time step.
   216→Errors from earlier steps therefore carry forward without growth and simply add to
   217→the new local error. We now make this point explicit in the proof of the global
   218→error bound in Section~4.
   219→
   220→\medskip
   221→
   222→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.4:} \textit{Certain fringe models with ``bottleneck reactions'' might be
   223→nontrivial with any FSP with time-stepping or sliding windows, including the
   224→method in this paper.}
   225→
   226→\textbf{Response:} We are very grateful for this comment; it directly motivated one of
   227→the central case studies in the revised manuscript.
   228→
   229→Section~5.1 now presents a detailed bottleneck example along the lines you
   230→described. We consider a three-species system with a slow activation step and a
   231→fast production step leading to an advancing front in $C$. The parameters are
   232→chosen so that the intermediate states on the activation path have extremely low
   233→probability but carry the only significant flux into regions with large $C$.
   234→
   235→In this setting we compare:
   236→\begin{itemize}
   237→  \item a probability-only variant (quantile pruning without the flux safeguard), and
   238→  \item the full flux-preserving algorithm (flux-based pruning combined with the
   239→        flux-adaptive time-stepping rule of Section~3).
   240→\end{itemize}
   241→
   242→The results in Section~5.1 (Figure~4 and Tables~1--2) show that the
   243→probability-only variant quickly removes bottleneck states from the truncated set,
   244→after which the numerical solution remains localized near the initial state and
   245→fails to reproduce the growth of $C$. In contrast, the flux-based variant
   246→retains bottleneck states whenever their exit flux is a non-negligible fraction
   247→of the total system flux, and it reproduces the expected increase in
   248→$\langle C\rangle$ over several orders of magnitude in time. This example
   249→illustrates precisely the pathology you raised and shows that the flux safeguard
   250→is effective in protecting such bottleneck channels.
   251→
   252→\medskip
   253→
   254→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.5:} \textit{Can the authors compare their method to previous FSP methods that
   255→also incorporate adaptive state spaces, either in discussion or numerical tests?
   256→Some are already cited in the paper. Another paper that comes to mind is Dinh \&
   257→Sidje (Physical Biology, 2017).}
   258→
   259→\textbf{Response:} We have expanded the discussion of related work in the Introduction
   260→(Related Work subsection) and in Section~5 to position the revised method more
   261→clearly among existing approaches.
   262→
   263→In particular, we now discuss:
   264→\begin{itemize}
   265→  \item Aggregation and lumping methods such as those of Bobbio \& Trivedi and
   266→        Zhang, Watson, \& Cao, which group micro-states into macro-states using
   267→        stationary or Monte Carlo information.
   268→  \item Sliding-window and hybrid FSP--SSA schemes such as those by Wolf
   269→        et al.\ and MacNamara et al., which track moving regions of support or
   270→        couple deterministic and stochastic updates.
   271→  \item Krylov-FSP-SSA and tensor-train methods of Dinh \& Sidje and
   272→        collaborators, which guide state-space expansion using SSA trajectories or
   273→        compressed representations.
   274→\end{itemize}
   275→
   276→Our flux-based adaptive FSP differs in two main ways:
   277→
   278→\begin{enumerate}
   279→  \item In the analysis, we control truncation error using flux across the
   280→        active--inactive boundary, which leads directly to the local and global
   281→        error bounds in Section~4. In the algorithm, we approximate this boundary
   282→        activity using statewise exit flux as the main control quantity rather
   283→        than relying on stationary information.
   284→  \item We decouple discovery of new states (via reachability expansion of the
   285→        reaction network) from the pruning decision, using quantiles only as a
   286→        pre-selection mechanism and flux as the final safeguard. This explicitly
   287→        addresses the bottleneck scenario highlighted by Reviewer~1.
   288→\end{enumerate}
   289→
   290→Implementing and tuning several competing adaptive FSP codes for a full numerical
   291→benchmark on all our examples would require substantial additional effort and is
   292→beyond the scope of the current revision. Instead, we focus on clearly articulating
   293→the conceptual differences and providing detailed algorithmic descriptions and
   294→performance data that we hope will make future comparisons easier.
   295→
   296→\medskip
   297→
   298→\noindent\textbf{Comment 1.6:} \textit{Although well studied, Michaelis--Menten, Lotka--Volterra, and toggle
   299→switch models are relatively simple to solve. It would be beneficial to showcase
   300→your algorithm with at least one example where the state space is known to be
   301→large. Can the authors implement such a model?}
   302→
   303→\textbf{Response:} We agree that more demanding examples are essential. The revised
   304→manuscript now contains several such systems and explicitly orders them so that
   305→the bottleneck example and its error analysis appear first in Section~5.1, followed by
   306→the toggle switch and higher-dimensional models.
   307→
   308→\begin{itemize}
   309→  \item Section~5.1 presents the bottleneck reaction network and, in the
   310→        ``Experimental Error Analysis'' subsubsection, compares the flux-based
   311→        adaptive FSP to a high-accuracy fixed-FSP reference on the bounded state
   312→        space $\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,10000\}$. Figure~5
   313→        shows that the relative error in $\langle C\rangle$ remains below $0.1\%$
   314→        and decreases to about $0.015\%$ as the distribution spreads, with an
   315→        approximately constant instantaneous error rate in time, in agreement with
   316→        the additive error structure proved in Section~4. Table~3 reports mean
   317→        values and errors for all species at $t=10^5$ s; the adaptive and
   318→        reference solutions are in close agreement, with the adaptive state space
   319→        about $4.5$ times smaller than the fixed one.
   320→  \item Section~5.2 revisits the stochastic toggle switch, now primarily as a
   321→        qualitative illustration of bistability and basin switching under
   322→        flux-preserving truncation (Figure~6).
   323→  \item Section~5.3 introduces the Oregonator model of chemical oscillations.
   324→        Based on observed mean trajectory ranges, a conservative rectangular
   325→        bounding box would contain on the order of
   326→        $4{,}000\times 7{,}000\times 11{,}000 \approx 3\times 10^{11}$ states,
   327→        whereas the adaptive FSP keeps between a few dozen and a few thousand
   328→        states active at any time, achieving a compression ratio of roughly
   329→        $10^8{:}1$ while faithfully reproducing the oscillatory dynamics
   330→        (Figure~7).
   331→  \item Section~5.4 adds the Robertson (ROBER) autocatalytic system, which
   332→        is extremely stiff, with reaction rates spanning nine orders of magnitude.
   333→        Using the conservation law $N_A+N_B+N_C=10{,}000$ and the observed ranges
   334→        for $N_A$ and $N_B$, a conservative rectangular bounding box would contain
   335→        on the order of $10^5$ states, whereas the adaptive state space in our
   336→        simulations remains in the range $50$--$2{,}000$ states. Thus the method
   337→        achieves a compression of about two orders of magnitude while capturing
   338→        the three-phase dynamics (slow initiation, explosive autocatalysis, and
   339→        long equilibration) and controlling local boundary flux and time-stepping
   340→        error (Figure~8).
   341→\end{itemize}
   342→
   343→
   344→%======================================================================
   345→\section*{Response to Reviewer 2}
   346→%======================================================================
   347→
   348→\subsection*{Main Comments}
   349→
   350→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.1:} \textit{The first experiment, depicted in Figure 2, requires a much deeper
   351→discussion. The error seems to increase with time, contradicting the analysis.
   352→Also, 1000 SSA trajectories would not be enough to eliminate statistical error.}
   353→
   354→\textbf{Response:} We agree that the original SSA-based experiment did not clearly
   355→separate truncation error from Monte Carlo sampling error, and that the discussion
   356→of error growth was incomplete.
   357→
   358→In the revised manuscript we have replaced this experiment with a deterministic
   359→error study that directly tests the theoretical results:
   360→
   361→\begin{itemize}
   362→  \item Section~5.1.1 (Experimental Error Analysis) compares the flux-based
   363→        adaptive FSP to a high-accuracy fixed-FSP reference on the bounded state
   364→        space $\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,2\}\times\{0,\dots,10000\}$.
   365→  \item Figure~5 shows that the relative error in $\langle C\rangle$ remains below
   366→        $0.1\%$ and decreases to about $0.015\%$ as the distribution spreads, with
   367→        an approximately constant instantaneous error rate in time, in agreement
   368→        with the additive error structure in Section~4.
   369→  \item Table~3 reports mean values and errors for all species at $t=10^5$ s, with
   370→        the adaptive and reference solutions in close agreement and the adaptive
   371→        state space about $4.5$ times smaller than the fixed one.
   372→\end{itemize}
   373→
   374→We believe this new experiment more directly and transparently validates the
   375→revised error analysis and avoids conflating truncation error with statistical
   376→sampling error.
   377→
   378→\medskip
   379→
   380→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.2:} \textit{For most (if not all) experiments, the pruning factor $\alpha$, the
   381→effective pruned fraction $m$, and the time step are not reported. These should
   382→be specified in the paper rather than needing to be inferred from the code.}
   383→
   384→\textbf{Response:} We have revised the numerical sections to state the key algorithmic
   385→parameters explicitly:
   386→
   387→\begin{itemize}
   388→  \item Section~3, which introduces the flux-preserving pruning algorithm, now
   389→        specifies the quantile tolerance $\alpha$, the flux tolerance
   390→        $\varepsilon_{\rm flux}$, and the bounds $\Delta t_{\min}$ and
   391→        $\Delta t_{\max}$ used in the bottleneck experiments, as well as the
   392→        functional form of the flux-based time-step rule.
   393→  \item Section~5.1.1 provides the time grid and state-space bounds for the
   394→        fixed-FSP reference solution, and the adaptive time-step settings for the
   395→        comparison run in the bottleneck error study.
   396→  \item The later subsections of Section~5 (toggle switch, Oregonator, and ROBER)
   397→        state the choices of $\alpha$, flux tolerance, and time-step range used in
   398→        each example. The figures also show the resulting adaptive time steps and
   399→        state-space sizes as functions of time.
   400→\end{itemize}
   401→
   402→In the revised method, $\alpha$ primarily determines how much probability mass is
   403→eligible for pruning per step, while the flux safeguard further constrains which
   404→of those states can actually be removed. Rather than reporting an effective $m$ at
   405→every time step, we focus on how $\alpha$, the flux threshold, and the boundary
   406→fluxes enter the local and global error bounds in Section~4.
   407→
   408→\medskip
   409→
   410→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.3:} \textit{I would like to see more explicitly the relation between the pruning
   411→factor $\alpha$ and the effective pruned fraction $m$. This relationship will
   412→affect both efficiency and accuracy.}
   413→
   414→\textbf{Response:} We appreciate this request and have clarified the role of $\alpha$
   415→in the revised algorithm.
   416→
   417→In the original quantile-only scheme, $\alpha$ directly controlled the fraction of
   418→probability mass removed at each pruning step, so $m \approx \alpha$. The new
   419→method introduces a flux-based safeguard:
   420→
   421→\begin{itemize}
   422→  \item The quantile parameter $\alpha$ selects a candidate set of low-probability
   423→        states whose cumulative probability does not exceed $\alpha$.
   424→  \item The flux safeguard then scans this candidate set and retains any state
   425→        whose outgoing flux exceeds a prescribed fraction of the total system
   426→        flux. These protected states are not pruned, regardless of their
   427→        probability.
   428→\end{itemize}
   429→
   430→As a consequence, the effective pruned mass $m$ is at most $\alpha$, and can
   431→be considerably smaller when bottleneck states are present. This behavior is
   432→illustrated in the bottleneck experiment (Section~5.1): even with a relatively
   433→large $\alpha$, the flux safeguard prevents removal of the intermediate bottleneck
   434→states and thereby limits $m$ while maintaining connectivity.
   435→
   436→The local error analysis in Section~4 makes explicit how the local model error
   437→depends on the pruned mass, the boundary fluxes, and the time step, thereby
   438→connecting $\alpha$ and $m$ through their impact on the flux-based error control.
   439→A full parametric study of $(\alpha,m)$ over many systems would significantly
   440→lengthen the paper; we therefore leave a more systematic investigation to future
   441→work.
   442→
   443→\medskip
   444→
   445→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.4:} \textit{The authors report runtimes for their new algorithm, but these are
   446→only average values on a single hardware platform. At least the hardware used
   447→should be mentioned, and runtimes should be compared to those of existing
   448→algorithms; probably higher-dimensional examples need to be studied as well.}
   449→
   450→\textbf{Response:} We agree that performance information and reproducibility are
   451→important. In the revised manuscript we have:
   452→
   453→\begin{itemize}
   454→  \item Specified the implementation details and hardware in the Numerical
   455→        Experiments section: all experiments were run in Julia using Expokit.jl
   456→        for Krylov-based matrix exponential computations, Catalyst.jl for
   457→        reaction-network modeling, and sparse matrices from the
   458→        \texttt{SparseArrays} standard library. Simulations were performed on a
   459→        MacBook Pro with an M1 Pro chip and 16\,GB of RAM.
   460→  \item Added a dedicated subsection on performance evaluation (Section~5.5), which
   461→        analyzes the performance of forward-enumeration matrix construction
   462→        compared to a standard backward-expansion strategy. At the kernel level,
   463→        benchmark plots show that, for the Oregonator model, forward enumeration
   464→        reduces the median time for generator construction from about
   465→        $8.91$\,ms to $0.62$\,ms, a speedup of roughly $14.4\times$. In terms of
   466→        total simulation cost, Figure~10 and Table~8 report that forward
   467→        enumeration yields speedups of about $3.9\times$ (Oregonator),
   468→        $3.5\times$ (ROBER), and $9.8\times$ (toggle switch) relative to a
   469→        reference implementation using backward expansion.
   470→\end{itemize}
   471→
   472→A direct head-to-head comparison with existing adaptive FSP implementations
   473→(e.g., Optimal FSP, Krylov-FSP-SSA, aggregation-based methods) on the same
   474→hardware would require reimplementing or interfacing with multiple external codes
   475→and carefully tuning each method for fairness. We view such a study as an
   476→interesting direction for future work and, for the present revision, focus on
   477→documenting the internal performance characteristics of the proposed algorithm.
   478→
   479→\medskip
   480→
   481→\noindent\textbf{Comment 2.5:} \textit{Include a test case where excessive pruning would be an issue but
   482→your new method avoids that problem.}
   483→
   484→\textbf{Response:} The bottleneck example in Section~5.1 was designed precisely to
   485→address this request (and the related concerns raised by Reviewer~1). This example
   486→became the starting point for shifting the scope of the paper toward stiff,
   487→multiscale systems where rare but dynamically essential transitions must be
   488→preserved.
   489→
   490→As described in our response to Comment~1.4, the bottleneck model contains
   491→low-probability states that form the only pathway to large $C$. Any scheme that
   492→prunes solely on probability is forced either to choose a very small $\alpha$
   493→(sacrificing efficiency) or eventually to remove these states and thus
   494→qualitatively change the dynamics. The flux-based adaptive FSP method, by contrast,
   495→monitors the outgoing flux from candidate states and protects those whose flux is
   496→non-negligible. The plots and tables in Section~5.1 show that the flux-based
   497→variant retains the bottleneck channel and recovers the correct long-time
   498→behavior, whereas the probability-only variant does not.
   499→
   500→%======================================================================
   501→\section*{Summary}
   502→%======================================================================
   503→
   504→To summarize, the revised manuscript differs substantially from the original
   505→submission. The main advances are:
   506→
   507→\begin{enumerate}
   508→  \item A flux-preserving adaptive FSP algorithm that augments quantile-based
   509→        pruning with a flux safeguard and a flux-guided time-step controller,
   510→        directly addressing the bottleneck failure modes pointed out by
   511→        Reviewer~1.
   512→  \item A new error analysis that expresses local model error in terms of
   513→        boundary fluxes and exploits semigroup contraction to obtain additive
   514→        global error bounds (Proposition~4.1, Corollary~4.2, Theorem~4.4, and
   515→        Corollaries~4.6--4.8 in Section~4). In the Discussion we also outline a
   516→        natural next step of relating our flux-based error control to spectral
   517→        quantities (e.g., spectral gaps) via ergodicity coefficients and
   518→        Cheeger-type inequalities.
   519→  \item A set of challenging numerical experiments, including a detailed
   520→        bottleneck case study and its error analysis in Section~5.1, a stochastic
   521→        toggle switch, the oscillatory Oregonator, and the stiff Robertson system,
   522→        each with explicit reporting of parameters, state-space sizes, and
   523→        observed behavior (Figures~4--8, Tables~1--3).
   524→  \item A performance study of forward-enumeration matrix construction that
   525→        demonstrates substantial speedups over a standard backward-expansion
   526→        approach (Figure~10 and Table~8 in Section~5.5).
   527→\end{enumerate}
   528→
   529→We hope that these changes fully address the reviewers’ concerns and that the
   530→revised manuscript is now suitable for publication in \emph{Multiscale Modeling
   531→and Simulation}. We are very grateful to both reviewers and to the Associate
   532→Editor for their detailed and thoughtful feedback, which has been instrumental in
   533→improving this work.
   534→
   535→\vspace{1em}
   536→\noindent Sincerely,\\[0.5em]
   537→Aditya Dendukuri, Shivkumar Chandrasekaran, and Linda Petzold
   538→
   539→\end{document}
